s: Which of the following is guaranteed as a Fundamental Right under Article 32(1) of the Constitution of India?
o: The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
The right to appeal against every decision of a High Court
The right to seek an advisory opinion from the Supreme Court on every constitutional matter
The right to move any subordinate court for enforcement of statutory rights
x: Article 32(1) guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III.
tq: Identify the precise constitutional guarantee rather than a broader appellate or advisory power.
sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

s:
Under Article 32(2) of the Constitution, the Supreme Court may issue which of the following for enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
1. Directions
2. Orders
3. Writs
4. Advisory opinions only
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: Article 32(2) empowers the Supreme Court to issue directions, orders and writs, including the five named writs. Advisory opinions are not included in this provision.
tq: Separate the enforcement remedies under Article 32 from the Supreme Court’s advisory jurisdiction.
sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 32(3) of the Constitution:
1. Parliament may empower any other court to exercise some of the powers of the Supreme Court under Article 32.
2. Parliament has so far enacted a law empowering subordinate courts to issue writs under Article 32.
3. High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower other courts, but no such law has been made so far. High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
tq: Watch for the trap that changes a constitutional enabling provision into an enacted law.
sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes Article 32(4) of the Constitution of India?
o: The right under Article 32 is available only during a National Emergency
The right under Article 32 shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided by the Constitution
The right under Article 32 may be suspended by an ordinary law of Parliament
The right under Article 32 can never be suspended under any circumstances
x: Article 32(4) provides that the right guaranteed by Article 32 shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided by the Constitution.
tq: Distinguish constitutional limitation from absolute or ordinary-legislative restrictions.
sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following statements best expresses the constitutional position of Article 32?
o: It is a statutory remedy created by Parliament and may be withdrawn by Parliament
It can be completely repealed by a constitutional amendment because it is procedural
It forms part of the basic structure and cannot be abridged even by a constitutional amendment
It applies only to legal rights created by ordinary legislation
x: Article 32 is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. Its essential guarantee cannot be abridged even through a constitutional amendment.
tq: Use the basic-structure doctrine to reject options treating a Fundamental Right as an ordinary statutory remedy.
sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

s: The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 is best described as
o: original and exclusive
advisory but not original
original but not exclusive
appellate and exclusive
x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights, but this jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
tq: Split the paired descriptions—original and exclusive—instead of assuming that direct jurisdiction is exclusive.
sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

s: A person seeks enforcement of a right created only by an ordinary statute, without alleging violation of a Fundamental Right. Which of the following is correct?
o: Article 32 is not the appropriate remedy because it enforces only Fundamental Rights
Article 32 automatically converts the statutory right into a Fundamental Right
The person can directly invoke Article 32 as a matter of right
Article 32 can be invoked only if the President permits it
x: Article 32 is confined to enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Statutory rights and other non-Fundamental constitutional rights cannot ordinarily be enforced under Article 32.
tq: Apply the scope of the remedy to distinguish Fundamental Rights from statutory rights.
sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the writ of Prohibition?
o: Issued against a private person to compel performance of a contract
Issued by a higher court to stop a lower judicial or quasi-judicial body from exceeding its jurisdiction
Issued to test the legality of a person’s claim to a public office
Issued to release a person from every form of lawful detention
x: Prohibition is issued by a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal with judicial or quasi-judicial functions from exceeding its jurisdiction.
tq: Match the writ with the body against which it operates and the stage at which it acts.

s: A writ of Prohibition does NOT ordinarily lie against which of the following?
o: A judicial body
A quasi-judicial tribunal
An administrative authority acting administratively
A lower court exceeding its jurisdiction
x: Prohibition lies against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, but not against administrative authorities acting in an administrative capacity. It also does not lie against legislative bodies or private persons.
tq: Find the body outside the judicial or quasi-judicial field.
sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

s: Which statement regarding Certiorari is correct?
o: It is confined exclusively to private disputes between individuals
It can be issued only before a lower court begins proceedings
It may transfer a case or quash an order of a lower court or authority
It is available only against a legislative body
x: Certiorari may be used to transfer a case from, or quash an order of, a lower court or authority. It operates against judicial, quasi-judicial and certain administrative bodies affecting rights.
tq: Distinguish the corrective function of Certiorari from the preventive function of Prohibition.

s: Since 1991, the writ of Certiorari may also lie against
o: Certain administrative bodies when their actions affect rights
All legislative bodies without exception
Every private individual
The President and Governor for their official acts
x: The scope of Certiorari has been extended to certain administrative bodies whose decisions affect rights. It does not ordinarily lie against private persons or legislative bodies.
tq: Use the date-linked expansion of jurisdiction to identify the precise category added.
sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

s: Mandamus does NOT ordinarily lie against which of the following?
o: The President or Governor for official acts
An inferior court failing to perform a public legal duty
A public corporation
A public official
x: Mandamus may lie against public officials, public corporations, inferior courts, tribunals and government authorities, but not against the President or Governor for their official acts. Article 361 protects them from being answerable to any court for official acts.
tq: Apply the question ‘who would perform this public duty?’ and remember the constitutional protection of the President and Governors.
sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following is a limitation on the issue of Mandamus?
o: It may be issued only by a subordinate civil court
It may be issued against a private individual for any personal dispute
It is not issued to enforce a merely discretionary duty or a private contractual obligation
It may be issued to enforce every private contractual obligation
x: Mandamus enforces a public legal duty. It does not ordinarily lie for a merely discretionary duty, a private contractual obligation, non-statutory instructions or against private persons.
tq: Distinguish a public legal duty from a private or discretionary obligation.
sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to Habeas Corpus, consider the following statements:
1. It may be directed against public authorities.
2. It may also be directed against a private individual who unlawfully detains another person.
3. It necessarily results in release even when the detention is lawful.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Habeas Corpus may be issued against public authorities and private individuals for unlawful detention. It does not require release where the detention is lawful.
tq: Separate the persons against whom the writ lies from the condition that makes detention unlawful.
sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

s: Habeas Corpus does NOT ordinarily lie in respect of
o: Illegal detention by a private individual
Illegal detention by a public authority
Lawful detention or detention pursuant to a valid court order
A demand to produce a detained person before the court
x: Habeas Corpus is a remedy against unlawful detention. It does not lie against lawful detention, contempt of court or legislature, or detention outside the jurisdiction of the court.
tq: Look for the legality of detention before deciding whether Habeas Corpus is available.
sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

s: A person challenges the occupation of a substantive public office created by the Constitution. Who may ordinarily seek a writ of Quo Warranto?
o: Any interested person, even if not personally aggrieved
Only a member of the concerned legislature
Only the person personally aggrieved by the appointment
Only the Attorney-General of India
x: Quo Warranto may be sought by any interested person; personal aggrievement is not an essential requirement. The writ tests the legality of a person’s claim to a substantive public office.
tq: Use the standing rule to avoid importing the personal-aggrievement requirement of private litigation.
sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

s: Quo Warranto does NOT ordinarily lie in relation to
o: An unlawful claim to a public office
A private office or a merely ministerial office
A substantive office created by the Constitution
A substantive office created by statute
x: Quo Warranto examines the legality of a claim to a substantive public office created by the Constitution or a statute. It does not lie against a private or merely ministerial office.
tq: First identify whether the office is substantive and public before applying Quo Warranto.
sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

s: The writ jurisdiction of Indian constitutional courts is historically derived from the
o: English law of prerogative writs issued in the name of the King
Roman law of civil obligations
United States doctrine of judicial review alone
French system of administrative courts
x: The writs were borrowed from English law, where they were known as prerogative writs of the King, regarded as the fountain of justice.
tq: Identify the constitutional borrowing by linking the writs with their historical institutional source.

s:
Which of the following statements regarding writ jurisdiction in India is correct?
1. Before 1950, the High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras could issue writs.
2. Article 226 now empowers all High Courts to issue writs.
3. Article 226 confines High Court writ jurisdiction exclusively to Fundamental Rights.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Before 1950, the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts had writ jurisdiction. Article 226 now empowers all High Courts, and their jurisdiction extends beyond Fundamental Rights to other purposes as well.
tq: Reject the extreme word ‘exclusively’ by comparing the wider scope of Article 226 with Article 32.
sec: Guardian of Fundamental Rights; number of writs  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the institutional position regarding protection of Fundamental Rights?
o: Only Parliament is the protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights
The President is the final guardian of Fundamental Rights
Only the Supreme Court can protect Fundamental Rights
The Supreme Court is the protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights, while High Courts also share this role under Article 226
x: The judiciary, particularly the Supreme Court, is the protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights. High Courts also exercise this role through their jurisdiction under Article 226.
tq: Distinguish the principal constitutional guardian from the authorities that make or implement laws.
sec: Guardian of Fundamental Rights; number of writs  [APPSC]

s: How many writs are specifically recognised for enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32(2)?
o: Three
Six
Four
Five
x: Article 32(2) refers to five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.
tq: Count the constitutionally named writs rather than adding other judicial remedies.
sec: Guardian of Fundamental Rights; number of writs  [APPSC]

s: Which writ is traditionally regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty?
o: Quo Warranto
Prohibition
Habeas Corpus
Mandamus
x: Habeas Corpus is regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty because it provides a prompt judicial remedy against unlawful detention.
tq: Associate the liberty-protection function with the writ directed against unlawful detention.
sec: Guardian of Fundamental Rights; number of writs  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following statements regarding a writ of mandamus is correct?
o: It can be issued even when no governmental policy exists, to compel formulation of a policy.
It is issued exclusively against private individuals for performance of personal duties.
It may be issued to the Government to enact a law whenever a court considers the existing law inadequate.
It cannot compel the Government to make a law, but once a policy is laid down, its terms may be enforced through mandamus.
x: Mandamus cannot be used to compel the Government to make a law or formulate a policy. However, after a policy is laid down, its enforceable terms may be implemented through mandamus.
tq: Test the precise limit of a constitutional remedy rather than accepting an expansive power.
sec: Mandamus limits - making law, policy, private bodies  [APPSC]

s: Mandamus may NOT ordinarily be issued against which one of the following?
o: A public authority for failure to perform a statutory duty
A government department for breach of an enforceable policy
A private individual for enforcement of a purely private obligation
A public authority for failure to perform a mandatory public duty
x: Mandamus is generally directed against public authorities for public or statutory duties. It is not ordinarily available against private individuals or bodies for purely private obligations.
tq: Find the option involving a private obligation, which falls outside mandamus.
sec: Mandamus limits - making law, policy, private bodies  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding mandamus:
1. It may be issued against a private individual or body as a general rule.
2. It is not issued to enforce a discretionary duty.
3. It is not issued to enforce a legislative function.
4. It may be issued to enforce a non-statutory departmental instruction in every case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
x: Mandamus is not ordinarily issued against private bodies, for discretionary functions, legislative functions or non-statutory departmental instructions. Statements 2 and 3 correctly state its limitations.
tq: Split the options by identifying the statements that describe limits on mandamus.
sec: Mandamus limits - making law, policy, private bodies  [APPSC]

s: Which writ can, in appropriate circumstances, run against a private person?
o: Prohibition
Certiorari
Habeas corpus
Mandamus
x: Habeas corpus may be issued even against a private person who unlawfully detains another. The other writs are ordinarily directed against public, judicial or quasi-judicial authorities.
tq: Use the exceptional private-person feature to distinguish habeas corpus from the other writs.
sec: Mandamus limits - making law, policy, private bodies  [APPSC]

s: A High Court dismisses a writ petition on merits. The petitioner then approaches the Supreme Court under Article 32 on the same plea. What is the correct legal position?
o: The petition is automatically converted into a petition under Article 226.
The Supreme Court must hear the petition because Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
The petition is maintainable because res judicata applies only to civil suits.
The petition under Article 32 is barred by res judicata and the remedy lies only by way of appeal.
x: When a High Court dismisses a writ petition on merits, the same plea cannot ordinarily be raised before the Supreme Court under Article 32; the appropriate course is an appeal. If the dismissal was not on merits, a petition under Article 32 may be moved.
tq: Apply the res judicata distinction between dismissal on merits and dismissal on a technical ground.
sec: Mandamus limits - making law, policy, private bodies  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes prohibition from certiorari?
o: Prohibition is curative only, whereas certiorari is preventive only.
Prohibition is issued after final decision, whereas certiorari is issued only before proceedings begin.
Prohibition prevents continuation of proceedings, whereas certiorari generally quashes an order already passed.
Both writs are issued exclusively against private bodies.
x: Prohibition is primarily preventive and stops a judicial or quasi-judicial body from continuing proceedings without or in excess of jurisdiction. Certiorari is generally curative and quashes an order already passed.
tq: Compare the stage and effect of the two writs instead of their common jurisdictional basis.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Prohibition is issued while proceedings are pending.
2. Certiorari is generally issued after an order or decision has been passed.
3. Prohibition directs the lower body to stop continuing the proceedings.
4. Certiorari can never be used in relation to a pending proceeding.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Certiorari is generally post-decision, but it may also be used to transfer a pending case; therefore statement 4 is incorrect.
tq: Watch for the absolute word 'never' in a comparison of writ stages.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Prohibition — curative writ quashing an order already passed
Certiorari — preventive writ directing inactivity only
Prohibition — writ issued while proceedings are pending
Certiorari — writ available only against private individuals
x: Prohibition is a preventive writ issued during the pendency of proceedings. Certiorari is principally curative, and neither writ is ordinarily directed against private individuals.
tq: Start with the sure stage-writ pair and reject reversed descriptions.

s:
With reference to prohibition and certiorari, consider the following statements:
1. Both may check excess of jurisdiction.
2. Traditionally, both are directed against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies.
3. Prohibition quashes an order already passed, whereas certiorari merely prevents future proceedings.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Both writs check jurisdictional excess, and traditionally both operate against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies. Statement 3 reverses their normal functions: prohibition prevents continuation, while certiorari quashes an order.
tq: Identify the reversed comparison in the third statement.

s: Since 1991, certiorari may also be issued against certain bodies performing which kind of function?
o: Administrative functions
Private contractual functions only
Diplomatic functions
Purely legislative functions
x: The scope of certiorari has extended, since 1991, to certain administrative bodies in addition to judicial and quasi-judicial bodies.
tq: Test the dated expansion of the range of bodies subject to certiorari.

s: The expression “bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention” is associated with which writ?
o: Prohibition
Habeas corpus
Certiorari
Mandamus
x: Habeas corpus safeguards personal liberty by requiring justification for a person's detention. It is regarded as the greatest safeguard against arbitrary detention.
tq: Associate the liberty-protection description with the appropriate writ.

s: Which one of the following statements about Article 32 is correct?
o: It is itself a Fundamental Right and enables enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
It is merely a discretionary statutory remedy available before the Supreme Court.
It can be exercised only after the High Court refuses relief under Article 226.
It enables enforcement of every legal right, whether or not it is a Fundamental Right.
x: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and provides a remedy before the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. It does not generally cover every statutory or legal right.
tq: Distinguish the constitutional status and narrower scope of Article 32 from Article 226.

s: Which of the following is the most accurate comparison between Articles 32 and 226?
o: Article 226 is a Fundamental Right, while Article 32 is a discretionary remedy.
Article 32 covers Fundamental Rights, whereas Article 226 also extends to “any other purpose”.
Article 32 is available for legal rights only, while Article 226 is confined to Fundamental Rights.
Both can be used only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
x: The Supreme Court exercises writ jurisdiction under Article 32 for Fundamental Rights. High Courts under Article 226 may issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, including legal rights.
tq: Use the scope distinction—Fundamental Rights versus Fundamental Rights plus legal rights.

s: A High Court may issue a writ beyond its territorial limits under Article 226 when—
o: the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises within its territory
the Union Government transfers the proceeding to it
the Supreme Court authorises it in every individual case
the respondent is located anywhere in India, irrespective of cause of action
x: A High Court ordinarily exercises Article 226 jurisdiction within its territory, but may do so beyond that territory where the cause of action wholly or partly arises within its territorial jurisdiction. This position followed the Fifteenth Amendment of 1963.
tq: Apply the territorial-jurisdiction rule by focusing on the cause of action.

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the territorial operation of writ jurisdiction is correct?
o: Article 32 operates throughout India, while Article 226 ordinarily operates within the High Court’s territory, subject to the cause-of-action rule.
Article 32 is territorially confined to the State in which the petitioner resides.
Article 226 operates throughout India without reference to territorial jurisdiction.
Neither Article 32 nor Article 226 has any territorial limitation.
x: The Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction extends throughout India. A High Court's Article 226 jurisdiction is ordinarily territorial, though it may extend where the cause of action arises within its territory.
tq: Compare the territorial reach of the Supreme Court and High Courts.

s: Which of the following statements is correct regarding suspension of remedies during a National Emergency?
o: The President may, under Article 359, suspend the right to move any court for enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights.
Article 226 is automatically suspended whenever Article 32 is suspended.
Only Parliament, and never the President, can issue an order under Article 359.
The President may suspend the Constitution itself by an order under Article 359.
x: During a National Emergency, the President may by order under Article 359 suspend the right to move any court for enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights. Article 226 is not automatically suspended as such.
tq: Identify the authority and the precise object of an Article 359 order.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 19 is automatically suspended during every National Emergency.
2. Article 19 is suspended only when the Emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression.
3. Article 19 is not suspended on the ground of armed rebellion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Article 19 is suspended only during an Emergency declared on the ground of war or external aggression. It is not suspended when the Emergency is based on armed rebellion.
tq: Reject the overbroad word 'every' and apply the emergency-ground distinction.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Article)
A. Article 33
B. Article 34
C. Article 35

List-II (Provision)
1. Restrictions on Fundamental Rights during martial law
2. Parliament’s exclusive power to legislate on certain Fundamental Rights matters
3. Restriction or abrogation of Fundamental Rights of specified forces

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Article 33 concerns specified forces; Article 34 concerns martial law; and Article 35 gives Parliament exclusive power over laws relating to certain Fundamental Rights provisions.
tq: Start from the distinctive martial-law pair and complete the remaining matches.

s: Under Article 33, Parliament may restrict or abrogate Fundamental Rights of members of which of the following categories?
o: Armed forces, paramilitary forces, police forces and intelligence organisations
Only members of Parliament and State Legislatures
Only judges of constitutional courts
All public servants without exception
x: Article 33 empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces, forces charged with maintaining public order, intelligence organisations and related services, including specified police and paramilitary personnel.
tq: Test the constitutional category of personnel covered by Article 33 without extending it to all public servants.

s: Article 35 vests the power to make laws on certain matters relating to Fundamental Rights exclusively in—
o: The President by ordinance alone
Parliament
State Legislatures
High Courts
x: Article 35 reserves to Parliament the power to legislate on specified matters, including those connected with Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34.
tq: Use the phrase 'rests only with' to identify the constitutionally designated law-making body.

s: The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 was curtailed by the Forty-second Amendment and restored by—
o: The Forty-third and Forty-fourth Amendments
The Forty-fourth and Forty-fifth Amendments
The Forty-first and Forty-third Amendments
The Forty-sixth and Forty-seventh Amendments
x: The Forty-second Amendment curtailed Article 226. The Forty-third Amendment of 1977 and the Forty-fourth Amendment restored the position by removing the relevant restrictions.
tq: Arrange the amendment sequence by identifying the curtailment first and restoration amendments after it.

s: Which of the following provisions was inserted by the Forty-second Amendment and subsequently omitted by the Forty-third Amendment?
o: Article 21A
Article 32A
Article 300A
Article 243G
x: The Forty-second Amendment inserted Article 32A, which restricted challenges to State laws under Article 32. The Forty-third Amendment of 1977 omitted Article 32A along with Articles 131A, 144A, 226A and 228A.
tq: Use the amendment-pair trap by distinguishing inserted-and-omitted provisions from later additions.

s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 32(3) is correct?
o: It prohibits Parliament from conferring writ jurisdiction on any court.
It permanently transfers the Supreme Court’s writ jurisdiction to the High Courts.
It authorises State Legislatures to amend Article 32 by ordinary law.
It enables Parliament to empower other courts to exercise writ jurisdiction for specified purposes.
x: Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower any other court to exercise powers within the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction, subject to constitutional conditions.
tq: Focus on the authority empowered to extend writ jurisdiction under Article 32(3).

s: The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 was held to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution in—
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973
Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration, 1978
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997
x: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the basic structure.
tq: Match the landmark case with the constitutional principle it established.

s: Which institution is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, with the Supreme Court acting as their protector and guarantor?
o: The Election Commission
The Inter-State Council
The Judiciary
The Union Public Service Commission
x: The Judiciary is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, and the Supreme Court has the constitutional role of protecting and guaranteeing those rights.
tq: Identify the constitutional institution associated with protection and enforcement of rights.

s: Public Interest Litigation primarily relaxes which traditional rule?
o: The rule that courts cannot issue writs against public authorities
The rule that Fundamental Rights are enforceable only by Parliament
The rule that judicial review is unavailable against administrative action
The rule that only the directly aggrieved person may approach the court
x: PIL relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi by permitting a public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of persons unable to do so themselves or for a larger public interest.
tq: Identify the procedural rule changed by PIL rather than confusing it with a substantive right.

s: Which of the following statements about Public Interest Litigation is correct?
o: PIL is itself a Fundamental Right guaranteed by Article 32.
PIL is a procedural tool intended to make the judiciary accessible to disadvantaged persons.
PIL can be filed only by the person whose Fundamental Right has been directly violated.
PIL abolishes the requirement that a genuine public interest must be shown.
x: PIL is not itself a Fundamental Right; it is a judicially developed tool that relaxes locus standi and facilitates access to justice in matters of public interest.
tq: Distinguish a procedural judicial device from a constitutionally guaranteed right.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: S.P. Gupta — 1981 and development of PIL principles
L. Chandra Kumar — 1981 and relaxation of locus standi
Sunil Batra — 1997 and basic structure of Article 226
P.N. Bhagwati — Forty-second Amendment to Article 226
x: S.P. Gupta (1981) is associated with the development of PIL and relaxation of traditional locus standi. Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer were important judicial proponents of this approach.
tq: Begin with the case-year pair and eliminate options that swap cases, judges and principles.

s: Which judges are particularly associated with the development and promotion of Public Interest Litigation in India?
o: Justices L. Chandra Kumar and S.P. Gupta
Justices P.N. Bhagwati and L. Chandra Kumar
Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer
Justices Sunil Batra and V.R. Krishna Iyer
x: Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer are particularly associated with relaxing locus standi and promoting PIL as an instrument of access to justice.
tq: Separate the names of judges from the names of cases associated with PIL.

s: The practice of treating letters and postcards as writ petitions is known as—
o: Advisory jurisdiction
Inherent jurisdiction
Appellate jurisdiction
Epistolary jurisdiction
x: Epistolary jurisdiction refers to treating letters or postcards addressed to the court as writ petitions where they disclose a serious matter requiring judicial intervention.
tq: Test the exact technical term for an unusual form of access to writ jurisdiction.

s: The case associated with the use of a prisoner’s letter as an example of epistolary jurisdiction is—
o: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
x: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration is associated with treating a prisoner's letter as a basis for judicial intervention, illustrating epistolary jurisdiction.
tq: Match the illustrative case with the procedural innovation it demonstrates.

s:
Assertion (A): A public-spirited person may approach the court through PIL on behalf of persons unable to approach it themselves.
Reason (R): PIL relaxes the traditional rule that only the directly aggrieved person can sue.
Choose the correct answer:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true, and the relaxation of traditional locus standi directly explains why a public-spirited person can bring a PIL for affected or disadvantaged persons.
tq: Check whether the reason explains the procedural consequence stated in the assertion.

s:
With reference to Article 29 of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Any section of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it.
2. Article 29 is confined exclusively to religious and linguistic minorities.
3. No citizen can be denied admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution on grounds only of religion, race, caste or language.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Article 29(1) protects the language, script or culture of any distinct section of citizens, and Article 29(2) prohibits denial of admission on the specified grounds. Article 29 is not confined exclusively to minorities.
tq: Separate the broad protection under Article 29 from the minority-specific protection under Article 30.
sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 29 and 30 of the Constitution of India?
o: Article 29 applies only to minorities, whereas Article 30 applies to every section of citizens.
Article 29 deals only with religious institutions, whereas Article 30 deals only with linguistic institutions.
Article 29 concerns conservation of language, script or culture and admission protection, whereas Article 30 concerns the establishment and administration of minority educational institutions.
Both Articles 29 and 30 confer identical rights on all citizens without distinction.
x: Article 29 protects the interests of any distinct section of citizens in language, script or culture and safeguards admission. Article 30 is specifically available to religious or linguistic minorities for establishing and administering educational institutions.
tq: Use the scope comparison: Article 29 is broader, while Article 30 is minority-specific.
sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

s: Which of the following is guaranteed by Article 30(2) of the Constitution?
o: The State shall not discriminate in granting aid to educational institutions on the ground that they are under the management of a minority.
The State shall provide compulsory aid to every minority educational institution.
Minority institutions are exempt from every educational regulation.
Only linguistic minority institutions are entitled to State aid.
x: Article 30(2) prohibits discrimination in granting aid to an educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a religious or linguistic minority.
tq: Focus on the prohibition against discriminatory aid, not on an absolute right to receive aid.
sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

s: The 44th Constitutional Amendment inserted which provision to protect a minority institution when its property is compulsorily acquired?
o: Article 32(1A)
Article 29(1A)
Article 31(1A)
Article 30(1A)
x: The 44th Amendment added Article 30(1A), providing that compulsory acquisition of property of a minority educational institution should not impair the right to establish and administer such institution.
tq: Match the amendment with the exact sub-clause rather than the neighbouring Articles on property and remedies.
sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

s: Article 30(1A) is principally intended to ensure that acquisition of property belonging to a minority educational institution does not
o: make the institution a State institution
affect the right to establish and administer the institution
remove the institution from the scope of Article 29(2)
require approval of the Election Commission
x: Article 30(1A), inserted by the 44th Amendment, protects the minority's right to establish and administer its educational institution even when its property is acquired, subject to compensation-related protection.
tq: Apply the constitutional protection to the consequence of compulsory acquisition.
sec: Articles 29-30 - language, script, culture, minority educational institutions

s: The reference made by the President to the Supreme Court in the matter of the Kerala Education Bill, 1957, was under
o: Article 131
Article 136
Article 143
Article 145
x: The Kerala Education Bill, 1957 was considered by the Supreme Court pursuant to a Presidential reference under Article 143.
tq: Distinguish the advisory jurisdiction under Article 143 from the Court's original and appellate jurisdictions.

s:
With reference to the decision in In re Kerala Education Bill, 1957, consider the following statements:
1. Minorities were recognised as having the right to establish educational institutions.
2. The State could attach reasonable conditions to the grant of aid.
3. The judgment held that minority institutions could never be regulated by the State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The decision recognised the right of minorities to establish institutions and accepted reasonable conditions attached to State aid. It did not grant immunity from every form of State regulation.
tq: Reject the absolute word “never” while retaining the two propositions supported by the case.

s: In St. Xavier's College v. Gujarat (1974), the Supreme Court held that regulations concerning a minority educational institution were permissible primarily for ensuring
o: State takeover of its administration
reservation of all seats for the State
standards and excellence in education
abolition of minority management
x: St. Xavier's College v. Gujarat protected the right to administer minority institutions but accepted regulations intended to maintain academic standards and educational excellence.
tq: Distinguish regulation for academic standards from interference with administration.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: P.A. Inamdar (2005) — Presidential reference under Article 143
In re Kerala Education Bill (1957) — 11-judge Bench and State-wise minority status
St. Xavier's College v. Gujarat (1974) — right to administer protected, subject to standards and excellence regulations
T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002) — seven-judge Bench and no State quota in unaided institutions
x: St. Xavier's College v. Gujarat held that the right to administer is protected, while regulations for standards and excellence are permissible. The other options interchange the holdings or procedural features of the cases.
tq: Find the correctly matched case and holding by separating the four landmark decisions.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002):
1. It was decided by an 11-judge Bench.
2. Minority status is determined State-wise.
3. Unaided institutions enjoy institutional autonomy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: T.M.A. Pai Foundation was decided by an 11-judge Bench. It held that minority status is determined with reference to the State and recognised autonomy for unaided institutions.
tq: Treat bench strength, territorial basis and institutional autonomy as separate statement checks.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in P.A. Inamdar (2005)?
o: A seven-judge Bench held that the State could impose its quota in unaided institutions without limitation.
A seven-judge Bench held that there could be no State quota or reservation in unaided institutions, contributing to the subsequent 93rd Amendment framework.
An 11-judge Bench abolished the distinction between aided and unaided institutions.
The Court held that minority status must be determined at the national level.
x: P.A. Inamdar was decided by a seven-judge Bench and held that the State could not impose its quota or reservation in unaided institutions. The decision was followed by the constitutional development associated with Article 15(5) through the 93rd Amendment.
tq: Combine bench strength, holding and constitutional consequence without confusing it with T.M.A. Pai.

s: The constitutional provision associated with the post-P.A. Inamdar development concerning reservation in educational institutions is
o: Article 19(1)(g) through the 44th Amendment
Article 14 through the 42nd Amendment
Article 30(1A) through the 86th Amendment
Article 15(5) through the 93rd Amendment
x: The development following P.A. Inamdar is associated with Article 15(5), introduced through the 93rd Constitutional Amendment.
tq: Separate the amendment linked to reservation in educational institutions from the amendments linked to property and education rights.

s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the comparative scope of writ jurisdiction in India?
o: High Courts can issue writs only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, whereas the Supreme Court can issue them for any legal right.
The Supreme Court and High Courts have identical writ jurisdiction in both territory and subject matter.
The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction is wider in territorial scope than that of High Courts.

High Courts have a wider subject-matter scope because they may issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for other purposes, while the Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction is for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
x: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, whereas Article 226 gives High Courts wider subject-matter jurisdiction by extending it to other purposes. The Supreme Court is wider territorially, while the High Court's power is not wider in territory.
tq: Split the comparison into territorial reach and subject-matter scope.

s: The Indian constitutional writs are principally derived from the
o: American Bill of Rights
French administrative law
English prerogative writs
Roman civil law
x: The writ jurisdiction incorporated into the Indian constitutional system is derived from the English prerogative writ tradition.
tq: Recall the legal source of the writs rather than their Indian constitutional Articles.

s: The statement that “a right without a remedy is a worthless declaration” most directly explains the constitutional significance of
o: Article 30 providing aid to minority institutions
Article 143 providing advisory jurisdiction
Article 32 making Part III rights judicially enforceable
Article 29 protecting admission to aided institutions
x: Article 32 provides a direct constitutional remedy for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, thereby making the rights in Part III effective rather than merely declaratory.
tq: Connect the general principle of remedy with the constitutional mechanism that enforces rights.

s: The Supreme Court agreed on 20 January 2026 to examine whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction in a matter involving challenges arising from
o: Kerala and Karnataka against a Bombay High Court ruling
Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling
West Bengal and Odisha against a Madras High Court ruling
Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh against a Delhi High Court ruling
x: On 20 January 2026, a Supreme Court Bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma agreed to examine the issue in appeals involving Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling.
tq: Use the place-and-issue pairing to distinguish the current writ-jurisdiction development.

s: Which one of the following current developments concerns the Supreme Court's examination of urgent constitutional remedies for threats to life and liberty?
o: A uniform reservation policy for all minority institutions under Article 30
An SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings under Articles 32 and 226
A constitutional amendment replacing Articles 32 and 226 with Article 131
A proposal to abolish High Court writ jurisdiction
x: The Supreme Court was examining an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings in matters involving threats to life and liberty, strengthening practical access to remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
tq: Identify the practical remedy being examined rather than confusing it with a change in constitutional text.

s: A proposal to treat religious-instruction schools under Article 26(a), instead of Article 30(1), was left for consideration to the
o: Ministry of Law and Justice
National Commission for Minorities
Ministry of Education
Ministry of Minority Affairs exclusively
x: The plea concerning treatment of religious-instruction schools under Article 26(a) rather than Article 30(1) was left to the Ministry of Education.
tq: Apply the “which authority handles the matter?” test to distinguish the concerned ministry.

s: As of 18 September 2025, the number of High Courts mentioned in the constitutional writ-jurisdiction context, along with their sanctioned strength, was
o: 25 High Courts and 1,122 judges
26 High Courts and 1,122 judges
25 High Courts and 1,222 judges
24 High Courts and 1,122 judges
x: The stated figures were 25 High Courts and a sanctioned strength of 1,122 judges as on 18 September 2025.
tq: Check the institution count and sanctioned strength separately, especially the close numerical distractors.

s: In the ED-West Bengal matter, the constitutional issue involved a contest between
o: an Article 136 appeal by the Centre and an Article 368 reference by the State
an Article 226 petition by the Centre and an Article 143 reference by the State
an Article 32 petition defended by the Centre and an Article 131 suit claimed by the State
an Article 30 petition by the Centre and an Article 29 claim by the State
x: The Centre defended an Article 32 petition, while the State argued that the dispute should proceed as an original suit under Article 131.
tq: Distinguish enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32 from intergovernmental original jurisdiction under Article 131.
